## Cluster processing

In this chunk, we start by leaving the SES variables in the dataset to see what happens. Then, we will remove them to see how they predict the clusters.

```{r}

set.seed(666)

# Cluster analsis do not work with NAs we decide to drop all Nas which is certainly not the best solution
work_df_test <- work_df %>% 
  drop_na() 
  
  

# Take a look at the data with skimr
library(skimr)
s <- skim(work_df_test)
print(s, include_summary = FALSE)


# Calculate the dissimilarity matrix using gower distance because we have a mix of categorical and numerical variables
# daisy

D <- daisy(work_df_test, metric = "gower", stand = TRUE)

# Use NbClust to determine the optimal number of clusters
sil <- NbClust(diss = D, # calculated distance matrix with "gower" distances
               distance = NULL, # NULL because we provide D
               method = "mcquitty", # linkage method (closest to PEM)
               min.nc = 2, # minimum number of clusters
               max.nc = 10, # maximum number of clusters
               index = "silhouette" ) 

sil$Best.nc # best k according to silhouette index
sil$All.index # all silhouette indices for all k's
# The 3 clusters solution seems optimal here

# Perform PAM clustering with k = 3
kmed <- pam(D, 
            k = 3, 
            diss = TRUE # dissimilarity matrix 
            )

aggregate(x = .~ kmed$clustering, # cluster variable
          data = work_df_test, 
          FUN = mean )
# Cluster 1: the average ones, Cluster 2: the less likely, Cluster 3: the certain ones.

# Visualize the clusters using t-SNE
library(Rtsne) # for performing low-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional data
tsne <- Rtsne(D, # distance matrix
              is_distance = TRUE) # calculate solution based on our distance matrix
tsne$Y |>
  data.frame() |> # convert from matrix to data.frame class
  setNames(c("X", "Y")) |> # naming variables
  mutate(cluster =
           factor(kmed$clustering)) |> # add/create variable with our clusters
  ggplot(aes(x = X, y = Y)) + # use ggplot for plotting
  geom_point(aes(color = cluster))




```

## Let's leave SES variables out to see how they predict

```{r}

work_df_cluster <- work_df %>% 
  drop_na() %>% select(-c(Educ3, BirthPlace3, Language3, Educ, Age, Primipare, TrustAssMat, Active, SingleMum))  # should I remove activity?
# Take a look at the data with skimr
library(skimr)
s <- skim(work_df_cluster)
print(s, include_summary = FALSE)

set.seed(1234)
D <- daisy(work_df_cluster, metric = "gower", stand = TRUE)

```

## Hierarchical clustering

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
# In this chunk, we perform hierarchical clustering using the agnes function from the cluster package.

# We apply agnes to the dissimilarity matrix with Gower
res.agnes <- agnes(D, diss = TRUE, method = "complete") # Diss = TRUE, indicates that we use a distance matrix 

plot(res.agnes,hang = -0.1, which.plots = 2, main = "") # plot the dendrogram

# Cut the dendrogram into 3 clusters, it seems to make sense based on the widest distance, but the 4 clusters solution could also make sense

# With 3 clusters
cluster.agnes <- cutree(res.agnes, k = 3) # cut the tree to four clusters

# check frequency of clusters
table(cluster.agnes)

# calculate the means of our variables according to our clusters
aggregate(x = .~ cluster.agnes, 
          data = work_df_cluster,
          FUN = mean ) 

# We find the same pattern


# With 4 clusters
cluster.agnes4 <- cutree(res.agnes, k = 4) # cut the tree to four clusters

# check frequency of clusters
table(cluster.agnes4)

# calculate the means of our variables according to our clusters
aggregate(x = .~ cluster.agnes4, 
          data = work_df_cluster,
          FUN = mean ) 

# there is one category, the last one that has an ok proba to want, but has low norms and do not know much, is more inactive and signle mum and realy believes in returns, has high trust, present oriented
```

### Fuzzy clustering

```{r}
set.seed(1245)
# Perform fuzzy clustering with k = 2
res.fanny2 <- fanny(x = D, # distance matrix
                   k = 2, # number of clusters
                   diss = TRUE, 
                   memb.exp = 1.3) # use dissimilarity matrix


# Calculate the average values of the variables for each cluster
aggregate(x = .~res.fanny2$clustering, 
          data = work_df_cluster, # data set
          FUN = mean) # function to apply
## We can interpret them as percentages because the variables are binary.


# Perform fuzzy clustering with k = 3
res.fanny <- fanny(x = D, # distance matrix
                   k = 3, # number of clusters
                   diss = TRUE, 
                   memb.exp = 1.3) # use dissimilarity matrix


# Calculate the average values of the variables for each cluster
aggregate(x = .~res.fanny$clustering, 
          data = work_df_cluster, # data set
          FUN = mean) # function to apply
## We can interpret them as percentages because the variables are binary.

```

# LCA

```{r}

# with most variables
set.seed(1995)

work_df_cluster_LCA <- work_df %>% 
  drop_na() %>% mutate(NormsOpposedN = as.factor(case_when(
    NormsOpposedN == 0 ~ "zero",
    NormsOpposedN == 1 ~ "1",
    NormsOpposedN == (2 | 3) ~ "2/3",
    NormsOpposedN == 4 ~ "4/5",
    NormsOpposedN > 5 ~ "more than 5")
  ), 
  KnowsCreche = KnowsCreche+1, 
  KnowsAssMat = KnowsAssMat+1, 
  Graduate = ifelse(Educ3 == "Graduate", 1, 0),
  Undergrad = ifelse(Educ3 == "Undergrad", 1, 0)) %>% 
  select(-c(Educ3, BirthPlace3, Language3, 
                           Primipare,
                          Active, Age)) # %>% # I keep single lù
#  mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.numeric)) %>% 

  # should I remove activity?
# Take a look at the data with skimr
library(skimr)
s <- skim(work_df_cluster_LCA)
print(s, include_summary = FALSE)

f <- cbind(Intention, NormsOpposedN, AffordSubsidiesBaseline, AffordNMCostWBBaseline, AffordOppCostBaseline, AffordNMCostCareerBaseline, AccessHoursBaseline, AccessInformalFullTime, LikertReturnHKBaseline, TrustCreche, TrustAssMat, KnowsCreche, KnowsAssMat, HighLowECECBaseline, NormsBaseline, LikertAccessInfoBaseline, LikertAccessSoc, AccessEasy5, PresentOrientation, ComputerYN)~Graduate + Undergrad

ch2 <- poLCA(f,work_df_cluster_LCA,nclass=2)
plot(ch2) # educ is negatively associated with being in the dont't want
# BIC 44377.12 // 43734.79

ch3 <- poLCA(f,work_df_cluster_LCA,nclass=3)
plot(ch3) # seems to be the best in terms of BIC
# BIC 44260.21 //  43625.28

ch4 <- poLCA(f,work_df_cluster_LCA,nclass=4)
plot(ch4)
# BIC(4): 44282.79 // BIC(4): 43556.85


# Three clusters is lower BIC -- if we remove Single Mum, 4 clust is better
# it is also interesting and looks like the HC
```
